TEXT: Title: none printed. Annotations in top right: "Budget: $10", "Burgers: $2", "Bus Tickets: 50 cents". Y-axis label: "Burgers" (ticks 0 to 6, step 1). X-axis label: "Bus Tickets" (ticks 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24). Point labels: A, B, C, D, E, F.

- A: 0 bus tickets, 5 burgers
- B: 4 bus tickets, 4 burgers
- C: 8 bus tickets, 3 burgers
- D: 12 bus tickets, 2 burgers
- E: 16 bus tickets, 1 burger
- F: 20 bus tickets, 0 burgers

The points are evenly spaced: each step of 1 burger corresponds to 4 bus tickets. The line has no other labeled data series or legend.

The endpoints are 5 burgers with no tickets (A) and 20 bus tickets with no burgers (F). The constant slope means that each burger given up frees enough money for four more bus tickets.

TYPE: Supply-demand/economic diagram (production possibilities frontier curve).

TEXT:
- Y-axis label: "Healthcare"
- X-axis label: "Education"
- Curve label: "PPF"
- Point labels: A, B, C, D, F
- Caption (printed): "FIGURE 2.3 A Healthcare vs. Education Production Possibilities Frontier. This production possibilities frontier shows a tradeoff between devoting social resources to healthcare and devoting them to education. At A all resources go to healthcare and at B, most go to healthcare. At D most resources go to education, and at F, all go to education."
- No numeric tick values are printed on either axis.

DATA:
- Single series: a concave, downward-sloping PPF curve running from A on the healthcare axis to F on the education axis.
- A: on the healthcare axis, with zero education (all resources to healthcare).
- B: ~ slightly right of and just below A on the curve; dashed guide lines drop from B to the education axis and run horizontally to the healthcare axis.
- C: intermediate point on the curve between B and D, with no dashed guides.
- D: near the education axis, lower on the vertical axis; dashed guide lines show its healthcare and education levels.
- F: on the education axis, with zero healthcare (all resources to education).

MEANING:
The figure shows a production possibilities frontier illustrating the tradeoff between healthcare and education output: producing more of one requires producing less of the other. The curve's bowed shape indicates that moving from all-healthcare (A) toward all-education (F) involves increasing opportunity costs as resources shift between the two sectors.

TYPE: Supply-demand/economic diagram (production possibilities frontier curve).

TEXT:
- Vertical axis label: "Healthcare"
- Horizontal axis label: "Education"
- Curve label: "PPF₂"
- Point labels: A, B, C, D, E₁, E₂, F, H₁, H₂, R
- Figure title/caption: "FIGURE 2.4 Productive and Allocative Efficiency"

DATA:
- The curve PPF₂ runs from A on the healthcare axis (top left) to F on the education axis (bottom right), bowing outward toward the origin-opposite corner.
- Points on the curve: A (on the healthcare axis, no education), B, C, D, and F (on the education axis, no healthcare).
- Point R lies inside the curve, at height H₁ on the healthcare axis and horizontal position E₁ on the education axis.
- Dashed guide lines mark H₂ (height of B and C on the healthcare axis) and E₂ (horizontal position of C on the education axis).
- Approximate positions: B and C sit at about the same healthcare level (H₂, ~ slightly above H₁), with C at education level E₂ (~ further right than E₁). D lies lower and further right than C along the curve.
- No numeric tick values are printed on the axes.

MEANING: All points on the frontier (A, B, C, D, F) show productive efficiency, since more of one good requires less of the other. Point R, inside the frontier at (E₁, H₁), is productively inefficient because both healthcare and education could be increased. The caption adds that allocative efficiency depends on which point on the frontier society most desires, so choosing among B, C, and D is a question of preference.

TYPE: Supply-demand/economic diagram (two production possibility frontier curves shown as side-by-side panels).

TEXT:
- Panel (a) axis labels: vertical "Sugar Cane"; horizontal "Wheat"; caption "(a) Brazil Production per acre (tons)"
- Panel (b) axis labels: vertical "Sugar Cane"; horizontal "Wheat"; caption "(b) U.S. production per acre (tons)"
- Point labels: Panel (a) "B" on the sugar cane axis and "A" on the wheat axis; Panel (b) "B" on the sugar cane axis and "A" on the wheat axis.
- Figure title (printed caption): "FIGURE 2.5 Production Possibility Frontier for the U.S. and Brazil"
- No tick values or numeric data labels are printed.

DATA: Each panel shows one concave production possibility frontier running from point B on the sugar cane axis to point A on the wheat axis. No numeric values are printed, so no values are given.

MEANING: The two panels compare production possibility frontiers for Brazil (a) and the U.S. (b). The U.S. curve is flatter, meaning it gives up less sugar cane per unit of wheat, so wheat has lower opportunity cost in the U.S. The Brazil curve is steeper, so sugar cane has lower opportunity cost in Brazil, which illustrates each country's comparative advantage.

TYPE: Supply-demand/economic diagram (two side-by-side economic diagrams: a straight-line budget/opportunity set and a concave production possibilities frontier).

TEXT:
Left panel: "Good 2" (vertical axis label), "Good 1" (horizontal axis label), caption "(a) An individual opportunity set".
Right panel: "Good 1" (vertical axis label), "Good 2" (horizontal axis label), caption "(b) A social production possibilities frontier".
Overall figure label/caption: "FIGURE 2.6 The Tradeoff Diagram. Both the individual opportunity set (or budget constraint) and the social production possibilities frontier show the constraints under which individual consumers and society as a whole operate. Both diagrams show the tradeoff in choosing more of one good at the cost of less of the other."
No tick values or numeric scales are printed on either axis.

DATA:
Panel (a): one straight downward-sloping line running from a point on the Good 2 axis (upper left) to a point on the Good 1 axis (lower right). Both intercepts are unlabeled; the line is linear, implying a constant rate of tradeoff between the goods.
Panel (b): one downward-sloping curve bowed outward (concave toward the origin) from a point on the Good 1 axis to a point on the Good 2 axis, with the curve steepening toward the Good 2 axis. Intercepts are unlabeled.

MEANING:
Both panels illustrate the tradeoff between two goods: any point on or inside the line or curve is attainable, and getting more of one good requires giving up some of the other. The straight line (individual opportunity set) shows a constant tradeoff for one consumer, while the bowed-out curve (social production possibilities frontier) shows that society's tradeoff changes along the frontier.

TYPE: Supply-demand/economic diagram (line graph with two intersecting curves).

TEXT:
Title: none printed. Figure caption: "FIGURE 3.4 Demand and Supply for Gasoline."
Y-axis label: "P ($ per gallon)". Y-axis ticks: $0.60, $1.00, $1.20, $1.40, $1.80, $2.20.
X-axis label: "Quantity of Gasoline (millions of gallons)". X-axis ticks: 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900.
Curve labels: "S" (supply, upper right), "D" (demand, lower right).
Point label: "E" (equilibrium).
Annotations: "Equilibrium price" (at $1.40), "An above-equilibrium price" (at $1.80), "A below-equilibrium price" (at $1.20), "Excess supply or surplus" (bracket between $1.80 points), "Excess demand or shortage" (bracket between $1.20 points).

DATA:
- Demand (D): ~$2.20 at ~420; ~$1.80 at ~500; $1.40 at ~600; ~$1.20 at ~700; ~$1.00 at ~800.
- Supply (S): ~$1.00 at ~500; ~$1.20 at ~550; $1.40 at ~600; ~$1.80 at ~680; ~$2.20 at ~720.
- Equilibrium E: $1.40, 600 million gallons.
- At $1.80: quantity demanded ~500, quantity supplied ~680, excess supply ~180.
- At $1.20: quantity demanded ~700, quantity supplied ~550, excess demand ~150.

MEANING: The demand and supply curves intersect at equilibrium E, where the price is $1.40 and quantity is 600 million gallons. Above equilibrium (at $1.80), quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus. Below equilibrium (at $1.20), quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage.

- Single series: a downward-sloping demand curve labeled D, running from upper left to lower right.
- One highlighted point on the curve at price P0 (dashed guide line extending horizontally from P0 to the curve) and quantity Q0 (dashed guide line extending vertically from the curve down to Q0).

The downward slope shows the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.
